draft.title: The bombing of Darwin
card: On 19 February 1942 Japanese aircraft bombed Darwin, a port town in the Northern Territory. It was the first time Australia was attacked directly by a foreign power in the war.
More than 230 people were killed. Ships in the harbour, the wharf, the town and the airfields were hit.
Darwin was a base for Allied ships and aircraft sent to defend nearby islands. Japan wanted to stop it being used to support Allied forces in the region.
It was the first of many raids on northern Australia. They went on until late 1943 and showed that the mainland was within reach of Japan.
draft.remember: Darwin was the first direct attack on Australia, and raids on the north followed.

a.q: Why was the bombing of Darwin a turning point for how Australians saw the war?
opts: It showed the mainland was within reach of Japan
It ended Japanese raids on northern Australia
It was the first battle fought by Australian troops
It forced Australia to leave the Allied forces
a.why: The attack was the first direct strike on Australia by a foreign power, so the war felt close to home. It was not the end of raids, because many more followed on northern Australia.
a.clue: Think about where the attack happened, not where troops had fought.

b.q: Which statement about the raids on Darwin and northern Australia is correct?
opts: The 19 February 1942 raid was the first of many
The 19 February 1942 raid was the only air attack
The raids targeted only soldiers and left towns alone
The raids began after Japan had already been defeated
b.why: The 19 February 1942 raid began a series of raids on northern Australia that lasted until late 1943. It was not the only one. It also hit the town, the wharf and ships in the harbour, so it was not aimed only at soldiers.
b.clue: Look for the option that says the raids continued.

a.best: It showed the mainland was within reach of Japan

b.best: The 19 February 1942 raid was the first of many

problems.detail: 'The first time Australia was attacked directly by a foreign power in the war' is imprecise. Australian-administered territories had already been attacked, such as Nauru in 1940 and Rabaul in January 1942. The usual accurate claim is the first attack on the Australian mainland.
'The first direct attack on Australia' repeats the imprecise claim. It should say the first attack on the Australian mainland.

The question calls the bombing a 'turning point' for how Australians saw the war, but the card never calls it a turning point. The card only says the raids showed the mainland was within reach of Japan.
The clue 'Look for the option that says the raids continued' points straight at 'first of many'. A student can pick it without knowing the content.

check.summary: The facts are sound apart from the claim of the 'first direct attack on Australia', which should say the Australian mainland, since Rabaul and Nauru were attacked earlier. Question b's clue gives the answer away, and question a's 'turning point' framing is not taught on the card.

proposal.title: The bombing of Darwin
card: On 19 February 1942 Japanese aircraft bombed Darwin, a port town in the Northern Territory. It was the first attack on the Australian mainland in the war.
More than 230 people were killed. Ships in the harbour, the wharf, the town and the airfields were hit.
Darwin was a base for Allied ships and aircraft sent to defend nearby islands. Japan wanted to stop it being used to support Allied forces in the region.
It was the first of many raids on northern Australia. They went on until late 1943 and showed that the mainland was within reach of Japan.
proposal.remember: Darwin was the first attack on the Australian mainland, and raids on the north followed.

a.q: What did the raids on Darwin and northern Australia show Australians?
opts: The mainland was within reach of Japanese attack
The mainland was too far away for Japan to reach
Japan was attacking only Allied ships out at sea
Japan was using Darwin as a base for its own ships
a.why: Japanese aircraft struck the Australian mainland again and again until late 1943, so the mainland was clearly within Japan's reach. The raids were not aimed only at ships at sea, because the town, the wharf and the airfields were hit too.

b.q: A student says, 'Darwin was bombed once in February 1942, and northern Australia was safe after that.' What is wrong with this claim?
opts: Raids on northern Australia went on until late 1943
Darwin was first bombed in 1943, not in 1942
The raid hit only ships, not the town of Darwin
Japan bombed Darwin to use the port for its own ships
b.why: The 19 February 1942 raid was only the first of many on northern Australia, and they lasted until late 1943. The date in the claim is right, so saying Darwin was first bombed in 1943 is wrong. The raid also hit the town, the wharf and the airfields, not only ships.
b.clue: Which part of the claim is about what came later?
